\subsection{Introduction}
\label{app:sec:intro}
% ============================================================

Vision-language-action (VLA) models that emit chain-of-thought reasoning alongside their action tokens are widely proposed as a route toward interpretable robotics: the reasoning is expected to expose the model's plan for review, correction, or safety monitoring \citep{ecot,cotvla,ecotlite,deepthinkvla}. This premise -- that the emitted CoT \emph{drives} the subsequent action decode -- underwrites downstream systems such as CoT-based safety monitors, CoT-edit-based corrective interventions, and CoT-derived auditing. Yet the premise has not been empirically evaluated for manipulation VLAs under uniform conditions. Recent work has evaluated CoT-faithfulness for driving VLAs \citep{vladrivebench,pinocchio} and probed CoT-based safety monitors under perturbation in a small manipulation cohort \citep{doubleedged}; a general, cross-model, cross-corpus, standardized benchmark for manipulation-domain CoT-faithfulness is missing.

We taxonomize the design space of CoT-faithfulness evaluation into three probe families (attention, causal-intervention, downstream-utility) and populate each with formal metrics, a null control, and reference implementations. Applied to 15 manipulation VLAs across 4 architecture families (OpenVLA non-CoT $\times 4$, DeepThinkVLA $\times 3$, our ECoT LoRA-fine-tune $\times 7$, ECoT-bridge public $\times 1$), CoT-Faith enables systematic study of \emph{which training regimes yield actually load-bearing reasoning}, distinct from \emph{which regimes surface-emit reasoning text}.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item {\bf CoT-Faith benchmark.} A standardized suite for measuring chain-of-thought faithfulness in manipulation VLAs, comprising ten edit families organized into a three-tier taxonomy (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), applied to $\sim 100$ LIBERO first-step samples per family per model.
\item {\bf Evaluation protocol.} A paired-intervention protocol with a formal Faithfulness Score $\mathcal{F}$ (Eq.~\ref{app:eq:faith}), a null selfsplice control that must show $\mathcal{F}\!=\!0$, an attention-decomposition probe with formal segment boundaries (Eq.~\ref{eq:attn}) reported in both total-mass and per-token normalization, three per-model calibration nulls that bound the score from below, and a direction-aware score $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ (Eq.~\ref{app:eq:fdir}) that requires the induced action change to point the way the edit implies.
\item {\bf Cross-family coverage.} 15 VLAs across 4 architecture families evaluated end-to-end under identical conditions: 4 OpenVLA non-CoT baselines (one per LIBERO suite), 3 DeepThinkVLA variants (base, SFT, RL), 1 public ECoT-bridge, and 7 of our LoRA variants. An $N{=}100$ sweep on 3 additional manipulation corpora (Bridge~V2, RT-1/Fractal, BC-Z) demonstrates protocol portability.
\item {\bf Public artifact.} We release all code, training checkpoints, per-sample action pairs with the edit metadata that regenerates each edited trace deterministically, per-episode attention logs, and the CoT-Faith leaderboard at [URL redacted]. All $\sim$27{,}000 evaluation calls reproducible from a single command.
\item {\bf Findings enabled by CoT-Faith.} Section~\ref{sec:analysis} details three controlled findings (F1--F3), one uncontrolled observation (O4), one cross-corpus transfer result (F5), one metric-level finding (F6), a second-architecture replication (F7), and one negative result (F8): (F1) attention on CoT is architecture-determined; (F2) causal effect requires reasoning-target training, though only in \emph{absolute} terms (Section~\ref{sec:f2_calib}); (F3) attention and causation are dissociated; (O4) a Bridge-corpus-trained model is $\sim 2\times$ more faithful than our LIBERO r=32 fine-tune on three shared edits, but this comparison conflates $15\times$ data quantity with target-corpus distribution and is reported as a training-regime \emph{observation}, not an isolated causal finding; (F5) attention profiles are cross-corpus stable at $N{=}100$ on 3 external corpora; (F6) \emph{magnitude-based} CoT-edit scoring --- the protocol used by this benchmark and its driving-VLA precedents --- ranks models in the \emph{opposite} order from direction-aware scoring, because a model earns credit for moving in any direction after a semantic reversal.
\end{enumerate}

% ============================================================
\subsection{Related work}
\label{app:sec:related}
% ============================================================

\paragraph{Manipulation VLAs with chain-of-thought.}
ECoT \citep{ecot} introduced the nine-tag reasoning trace (\texttt{TASK}, \texttt{PLAN}, \texttt{VISIBLE OBJECTS}, \texttt{SUBTASK REASONING}, \texttt{SUBTASK}, \texttt{MOVE REASONING}, \texttt{MOVE}, \texttt{GRIPPER POSITION}, \texttt{ACTION}) as the target during LoRA fine-tuning of OpenVLA-7B. ECoT-Lite / Efficient Embodied Reasoning \citep{ecotlite} released dense per-timestep reasoning annotations over 90 LIBERO tasks and studied training strategies for efficient embodied reasoning. DeepThinkVLA \citep{deepthinkvla} extended the framework with a hybrid-attention decoder (causal attention for language, bidirectional attention for parallel action decoding) on PaliGemma, plus a two-stage SFT-then-RL alignment pipeline. OpenVLA-OFT \citep{openvlaoft} proposed an Optimized Fine-Tuning recipe (parallel decoding, action chunking, continuous action representation) for adapting VLAs to new robot setups. All four assume that the emitted CoT informs the action.

\paragraph{Faithfulness in language models.}
For LLMs, \citet{turpin2023} showed that CoT can be post-hoc rationalisation; \citet{lanham2023} showed rank-based CoT importance is inconsistent across tasks. These motivate our manipulation-domain investigation.

\paragraph{Existing embodied CoT-faith work.}
VLADriveBench \citep{vladrivebench} defined the mentioning/hallucination/contradiction/action-alignment quartet plus a CoT-intervention protocol for autonomous-driving CoT-VLAs. Pinocchio \citep{pinocchio} operationalized a behavioral surrogate for embodied faithfulness through a learned critic scoring observation grounding and stepwise coherence on driving trajectories. \citet{doubleedged} evaluated three VLA reasoning designs (no-reasoning, text-CoT, latent-iterative) on LIBERO and SimplerEnv under vision/reasoning/action-stage perturbations and monitor-based defenses; their study focused on robustness under perturbation and did not include a null selfsplice control or a multi-family causal-edit taxonomy, and did not evaluate cross-corpus generalization of a CoT-driven action monitor.

\paragraph{Comparison with existing manipulation benchmarks.} Table~\ref{tab:compare} contrasts CoT-Faith with prior VLA benchmarks on the axes of faithfulness-specificity, edit-family coverage, statistical protocol, model-family and corpus coverage. CoT-Faith is the first to combine: (a) faithfulness-specific metrics; (b) $\geq 10$ edit families with a null control; (c) a same-base same-data reasoning-target ablation; (d) cross-corpus evaluation.

% ============================================================
\subsection{The CoT-Faith benchmark}
\label{app:sec:benchmark}
% ============================================================

CoT-Faith is designed around four selection principles: (P-1) \emph{faithfulness-specific:} each metric operationalizes CoT $\to$ action causal flow rather than surface task success; (P-2) \emph{null-controlled:} every metric has a validated null intervention with expected $\Delta\!=\!0$; (P-3) \emph{ablation-friendly:} models sharing base and data must be comparable, so training-target ablations are supported; (P-4) \emph{reproducible:} all edits, models, and metrics are code-released with a single-command reproduction of every reported cell.

\subsubsection{Task suite and prompt template}

We evaluate primarily on the Embodied-CoT LIBERO-90 dataset \citep{ecotlite}, which contains dense reasoning annotations across 90 LIBERO tasks spanning the four LIBERO suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, 10/Long). Each sample is a triple $(\text{img}, \text{instr}, \text{cot})$. The assistant turn follows the standard nine-tag ECoT template of \citet{ecot}:
\begin{center}\small
\texttt{USER: What action should the robot take to \{\allowbreak{}instr\}? ASSISTANT: TASK: \{\allowbreak{}...\} PLAN: \{\allowbreak{}...\} $\ldots$ GRIPPER POSITION: \{\allowbreak{}...\} ACTION: \{\allowbreak{}7 tokens\}}
\end{center}
Non-CoT baselines use the OpenVLA template, leaving the CoT segment empty. For cross-corpus evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:cross_corpus}) we use raw Bridge~V2, RT-1/Fractal, and BC-Z lerobot-format datasets and let each model \emph{self-generate} its CoT via greedy decode; the same edit protocol is then applied to the model's own reasoning.

\subsubsection{Edit taxonomy (three semantic tiers, ten families, three calibration nulls)}
\label{sec:taxonomy}

CoT-Faith organizes edits by \emph{semantic depth} of the intervention:

\paragraph{Tier 0 -- surface / control ($\times 3$).} Interventions that should have zero or maximal effect if the metric is well-behaved.
\emph{selfsplice\_control:} identity substitution (X$\to$X). \emph{syntactic\_scramble:} word-order shuffle within \texttt{MOVE} and \texttt{SUBTASK}, preserving content words --- and an LLM judge confirms it preserves \emph{meaning} at a rate of $1.000$ (Section~\ref{sec:judge_edits}), so it is best read as a second meaning-preserving family rather than as a structural edit. \emph{cross\_task\_swap:} replace the entire CoT with the reasoning from an unrelated LIBERO sample.

\paragraph{Tier 1 -- word-level semantic ($\times 4$).} Single-token or short-phrase swaps that mutate one semantic axis at a time. \emph{direction\_flip:} left$\leftrightarrow$right, up$\leftrightarrow$down, in$\leftrightarrow$out within \texttt{MOVE}. \emph{gripper\_flip:} grasp$\leftrightarrow$release, open$\leftrightarrow$close within \texttt{PLAN}/\texttt{SUBTASK}. \emph{verb\_swap:} action verbs $\to$ unrelated verbs --- though an LLM judge finds the swap actually changes meaning in only $0.575$ of pairs (Section~\ref{sec:judge_edits}), so this family is weaker than its name suggests. \emph{negation:} prepend ``do not'' to \texttt{SUBTASK}/\texttt{MOVE}.

\paragraph{Tier 2 -- object / causal-chain ($\times 3$).} Higher-order edits requiring cross-tag consistency. \emph{subject\_swap:} primary object referent $\to$ visible distractor across all reasoning tags. \emph{location\_swap:} spatial adverbs and 2-word location phrases within \texttt{PLAN}/\texttt{SUBTASK}/\texttt{TASK} (left/right, top/bottom, front/back, near/far, inside/outside, `left compartment' etc.). \emph{adversarial\_plausible:} object $\to$ second-most visible object, \emph{intended} to be visually plausible but wrong. An LLM judge confirms the referent changes ($0.958$) but rejects the plausibility half of that description: only $0.125$ of its edits are judged plausible (Section~\ref{sec:judge_edits}). We keep the family and the name, and readers should treat it as an unconstrained object substitution rather than as an adversarially plausible one.

\paragraph{Tier N -- calibration nulls ($\times 3$).} Meaning-preserving perturbations whose score defines each model's \emph{floor}. Every reported $\mathcal{F}$ must be read against them, and we treat them as first-class families rather than sanity checks. \emph{paraphrase\_null:} synonym substitution within \texttt{MOVE}/\texttt{SUBTASK} that preserves the instruction's meaning (\S~\ref{sec:paraphrase_null}). \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null:} $\pm 1$\,px perturbation of the \texttt{VISIBLE OBJECTS} bounding-box coordinates --- below the resolution the reasoning operates at. \emph{instr\_random\_sub:} 5-token random substitution in the \emph{instruction} rather than the CoT, which measures each model's global prompt sensitivity from \emph{outside} the CoT segment and so bounds how much of any CoT-edit score is CoT-specific at all. (\emph{selfsplice\_control} above is the fourth, degenerate null: exact identity, expected and observed $0.00$.)

Total: $\mathbf{10}$ edit families across three semantic tiers (of which \emph{selfsplice\_control} is the degenerate identity null, leaving $9$ non-null), plus $\mathbf{3}$ calibration nulls --- $\mathbf{13}$ families in all, matching Table~\ref{tab:compare}. Applied to $N{=}58$--$100$ LIBERO samples per model, with \emph{location\_swap} at $N\!\approx\!58$--$74$ after the annotation fix. \textbf{Coverage:} the calibration nulls have now been run on \textbf{all $\mathbf{11}$ models in the benchmark, in both architecture families} --- the seven ``ours'' leaderboard rows at 3 sampling seeds each, ECoT-bridge, an independent retraining of the no-CoT variant, and the three DeepThinkVLA checkpoints --- so every $\mathcal{F}$ in Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} has a measured floor and a measured ceiling from its own run, and the out-of-CoT specificity check is defined on every model (Table~\ref{tab:calibration}). One family is \emph{inapplicable} rather than unmeasured: \emph{bbox\_jitter\_null} perturbs bounding-box coordinates, and DeepThinkVLA's CoT renderer emits no bounding boxes, so the edit yields a byte-identical trace. The harness refuses to score an edit that does not survive rendering and records $n{=}0$ with all $100$ samples skipped, rather than returning the $\mathcal{F}=0.000$ that an unguarded run would report --- a number that is indistinguishable from \emph{selfsplice\_control} and would read as robustness where in fact no perturbation reached the model (\S~\ref{sec:f2_calib}).

\subsubsection{Faithfulness Score}

For each sample $s$ and edit family $f$, let $a(s, \text{cot}) \in \mathbb{R}^7$ denote the greedy-decoded action after de-quantising the 7 action tokens. The per-sample per-family faithfulness signal is
\begin{equation}
\Delta_\infty^{s,f} \;=\; \max_{i \in [7]}\bigl|\, a_i(s,\, f(\text{cot}_s)) - a_i(s,\, \text{cot}_s)\,\bigr|,
\label{app:eq:delta}
\end{equation}
where $a_i$ is the $i$-th action dimension normalized to $[-1, 1]$. A sample is \emph{faithful under $f$} iff $\Delta_\infty^{s,f} > \tau$, with $\tau = 0.05$ (5\% of the normalized action range). The \emph{Faithfulness Score} for a model $m$ on family $f$ is
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{F}(m, f) \;=\; \frac{1}{N} \sum_{s=1}^N \mathbf{1}\!\bigl[\Delta_\infty^{s,f}(m) > \tau\bigr].
\label{app:eq:faith}
\end{equation}
The overall Faithfulness Score is $\bar{\mathcal{F}}(m) = \tfrac{1}{|F|}\sum_{f \in F}\mathcal{F}(m, f)$, averaged over the 7 non-control edit families.

\paragraph{Null-control validation (two-fold, \S~\ref{sec:paraphrase_null}).}
\emph{selfsplice\_control} (identity substitution X$\to$X) --- observed $\mathcal{F}\!=\!0.000$ on 11/11 CoT-VLAs. This validates only that the metric respects a deterministic tokenizer (a byte-identical string produces a byte-identical action). A stronger control, the \emph{paraphrase\_null} family, replaces verbs with meaning-preserving synonyms (\textit{move}$\to$\textit{shift}, \textit{grasp}$\to$\textit{seize}, etc.) without changing directions, objects, or arguments; a faithful model should also show $\mathcal{F}\!\approx\!0$ under this edit, since the semantic content is unchanged. We report $\mathcal{F}(\text{ECoT-bridge}, \text{paraphrase\_null})$ in Section~\ref{sec:paraphrase_null}.

\subsubsection{Attention decomposition}
For an action-token source position $t \in \{T-6, \dots, T\}$, the attention mass on each segment bucket $B \in \{\text{visual}, \text{instruction}, \text{cot}, \text{action-prev}\}$ is
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\alpha(m, B) \;=\; \frac{1}{|L|\cdot|H|\cdot 7}
\sum_{\ell \in L}\sum_{h \in H}\\
\sum_{t=T-6}^{T}\sum_{j \in B} A_{\ell,h}^{(t,j)}(m),
\end{split}
\label{eq:attn}
\end{equation}
where $A_{\ell,h}^{(t,j)}$ is the attention weight from action position $t$ to key position $j$, and $L = \{0,1,2,3\}$ (early LLM layers) and $H$ are the 32 attention heads. The choice of $L$ is consequential and not innocent: over all $32$ layers the four buckets reorder (Section~\ref{sec:analysis}), so every $\alpha$ in this paper is an early-layer quantity and we report the full-depth values alongside.

\subsubsection{Attention-as-failure AUROC (P3): specified, withdrawn, and re-run in-domain}
For each sample the probe computes the L$_1$ error between the greedy-decoded action and the ground-truth demo action, binarizes at the median, and reports the non-parametric Mann--Whitney AUROC of $\alpha(m, B)$ as a per-sample failure predictor; a well-behaved attention-based interpretability metric should yield AUROC $\gg 0.5$. Unlike P1 and P2, this probe references \emph{ground-truth} actions and therefore inherits every normalization and convention mismatch between the model's training corpus and the evaluation corpus. Our first run violated exactly that constraint on two axes at once --- it scored a Bridge-trained checkpoint against LIBERO demonstrations, and it subtracted a \emph{normalized} predicted action from a ground-truth action in the robot's own units --- and we withdrew its numbers. The probe is now specified so that neither is expressible by accident: the predicted action is un-normalized with the checkpoint's own $q_{01}/q_{99}$ for the requested key, the harness \emph{raises} if the checkpoint carries no statistics for that key instead of falling back, and scoring a checkpoint outside its training corpus requires an explicit \texttt{-{}-allow-cross-domain} flag. The corrected in-domain run is reported in Section~\ref{sec:p3_indomain}, together with the withdrawn quantity recomputed on the same forward passes so the two protocols can be compared rather than merely contrasted in prose.

\subsubsection{Evaluation protocol}
\emph{Sample selection.} 100 first-step samples per condition; where compute permits, 3 file-shuffle seeds. \emph{Statistical protocol.} We report mean $\pm$ std across seeds where $\geq 2$ seeds exist --- which is now every row of Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} (all 8 CoT-VLA rows at 3 seeds) --- and single-run point estimates with Wilson 95\% CIs otherwise (the three DeepThinkVLA runs of Section~\ref{sec:cross_family}); Wilson intervals on the 3-seed rows are computed on counts pooled over seeds. For attention we separate sampling noise ($\sigma \leq 0.094$\,pp over 3 seeds at $N{=}100$) from same-config training-run noise ($0.12$--$1.95$\,pp over seven independent retraining pairs, one for every trained row), and compare model differences against the latter (Section~\ref{sec:analysis}). \emph{Reproducibility.} A single top-level script reproduces every reported cell in $\sim$3h on 8$\times$A100, and \texttt{scripts/\allowbreak{}verify\_\allowbreak{}paper\_\allowbreak{}numbers.py} re-derives each number quoted in this paper from the released JSON and exits non-zero on any mismatch.

\subsection{Model scores, and why we do not publish them as a ranking}
\label{sec:results}
% ============================================================

Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} reports the magnitude score $\mathcal{F}(m, f)$ for every model$\times$family cell we measured: rows are the 8 CoT-VLA models (non-CoT baselines have no CoT to edit and appear only in Fig.~\ref{fig:attention}), columns are the 10 non-null edit families plus one paraphrase-null (\emph{para}, Section~\ref{sec:paraphrase_null}) organized by tier. Fig.~\ref{fig:edit_heatmap} visualizes the same table as a heatmap. \textbf{Every row is a 3-seed mean$\pm$std} of a single 13-family run of that checkpoint, so every cell in the table carries an error bar and the \emph{para} floor is populated on all 8 rows.

\textbf{This table is a diagnostic, not a leaderboard, and the distinction is the paper's main methodological point.} Section~\ref{sec:paraphrase_null} makes a per-model paraphrase floor a \emph{required} field for admission to the public leaderboard. Seven of the eight rows below do not carry one, so \textbf{by our own admission rule seven of our own eight submissions would be rejected}, and the eighth --- ECoT-bridge, the only fully calibrated row --- has a floor that sits at the same height as its maximum-effect ceiling, which means its cells cannot be read as semantic sensitivity either. There is therefore no subset of this table on which a ranking is licensed, and we publish none: \textbf{no cell is bolded and the row order is the configuration order of Table~\ref{tab:models}, not a score order.} What the table is \emph{for} is the two structural findings it makes visible --- that magnitude scores can sit on an unmeasured high floor (F6, Section~\ref{sec:paraphrase_null}) and that they are direction-blind (Section~\ref{app:sec:directional}, final column). A reader who wants a comparative claim from CoT-Faith should take it from $\mathcal{F}_{\text{dir}}$ or from $\mathcal{F}_{\text{diff}}$, never from the magnitude cells.

% ============================================================
\subsection{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}
% ============================================================

We now use CoT-Faith to answer five questions about manipulation CoT-VLAs: three (F1--F3) that admit controlled comparisons under our benchmark, one (O4) that we treat as an uncontrolled observation because two axes are confounded, and one (F5) on cross-corpus transfer at $N{=}100$. Section~\ref{app:sec:directional} then re-examines all of them under a direction-aware scoring rule, which reverses the leaderboard ordering.

\subsubsection{F1: Attention on CoT is a floor set by architecture; training induces only a small shift}

Figure~\ref{fig:attention} shows the four-bucket action-token attention across 15 models. All 7 ECoT-family ``ours'' variants, \emph{including} the same-base same-data no-CoT variant, cluster tightly at $\alpha(m, \text{cot}) \in [0.335, 0.358]$ (max--min gap $= 0.023$ across r=8, r=16, r=32, r=64, no-CoT, data-50A, data-50B). All 4 OpenVLA non-CoT baselines read $\alpha(m, \text{cot}) = 0.000$, and this is \emph{definitional, not measured}: a non-CoT OpenVLA prompt contains no CoT segment, so the bucket has no tokens to place mass on and its value is $0$ by construction for any model of that architecture. It is therefore not an ``architecture floor'' in any empirical sense, and the OpenVLA-vs-ECoT bucket gap below is arithmetic rather than a finding --- we retain the comparison only to fix the scale of the four-bucket decomposition, and no claim in this paper rests on it. Within the DeepThinkVLA family, the base checkpoint exhibits $\alpha(m, \text{cot}) = 0.119$ and the two CoT-tuned variants exhibit $0.197$ (SFT) and $0.196$ (RL): a training-induced $+7.9$\,pp shift, showing training \emph{does} shift attention -- the cross-family difference is larger (23--29\,pp against OpenVLA), but as just noted that particular gap is definitional on the OpenVLA side and so is not evidence about training regimes; the informative cross-family comparison is ECoT ($0.335$--$0.358$) against DeepThinkVLA ($0.119$--$0.197$), both of which do emit CoT, and that gap ($14$--$24$\,pp) still exceeds the $7.9$\,pp training-regime shift. Note that on \emph{no} DeepThinkVLA checkpoint is the CoT bucket the largest: \texttt{action\_prev} leads on base ($0.384$) and \texttt{instr} leads on SFT and RL ($0.310$), so the CoT-bucket-dominance observation we report for the ECoT family at layers $0$--$3$ does not carry across architecture families either. The near-identical CoT attention on our no-CoT ($0.3491$) vs r=32 ($0.3543$, canonical run) --- same base, same data, action-only target vs full-CoT target --- puts the reasoning-target effect at $0.5$\,pp, and \emph{with the sign pointing the other way} than a reasoning-target story would predict. A second run of the same r=32 checkpoint gives $0.3398$, which flips the sign back and inflates the gap to $0.9$\,pp. Both are below our measured $1.45$\,pp run-to-run noise floor: the effect is \emph{indistinguishable from zero}, not merely small, and its sign is not even determined by our data. We report the canonical-run pair and claim no nonzero effect in either direction (see the noise-floor paragraph below). \textbf{F1: Among architectures that actually emit CoT, the architecture family accounts for more of the variance in $\alpha(\text{cot})$ than the training regime does; training-regime effects are second-order (across-family variance $<8$\,pp) or unresolvable at our resolution (within ECoT $<2.3$\,pp against a $1.45$\,pp noise floor).}

\paragraph{Per-token normalization: the CoT bucket is the largest only because it is the longest.} $\alpha(m, \cdot)$ in Eq.~\ref{eq:attn} is total attention \emph{mass} on a segment, and the four segments differ in length by up to $40\times$: visual $=256$ tokens (fixed), instruction $=59.5$ on average, CoT $=280.4$, action-prev $=7$. Dividing by segment length reverses the ordering entirely. For \mbox{r=32}: per-token attention is $0.00126$ on CoT tokens versus $0.00488$ on instruction tokens ($3.9\times$ higher) and $0.0103$ on the 7 previous-action tokens ($8.1\times$ higher); CoT tokens receive \emph{less} attention each than every other segment except visual ($0.00111$). The pattern is uniform across all 8 CoT-VLAs (per-token CoT $\in [0.00119, 0.00128]$, instruction $\in [0.00479, 0.00507]$). \textbf{So ``the CoT bucket carries the largest share of action-token attention ($\approx 0.34$)'' is a statement about how many CoT tokens there are, not about per-token salience, and we do not interpret it as evidence that the model attends preferentially to its reasoning.} We report both normalizations in the released per-model records (\texttt{per\_token} field). This does not weaken F1, whose content is a \emph{between-model} comparison at fixed segment lengths --- identical prompt template, identical $256$ visual tokens, and CoT length varying by $<2\%$ across the ECoT variants --- so the $23$--$29$\,pp OpenVLA-vs-ECoT gap and the $<2.3$\,pp within-ECoT spread are unaffected by the choice of denominator. It does mean the absolute bucket values should not be read as a salience ranking, and we have removed that reading wherever it appeared.

\paragraph{Attention noise, decomposed.} The within-ECoT spread that F1 calls ``negligible'' needs a noise floor, and the submitted version of this paper quoted a single $1.45$\,pp figure for it. That conflated two different quantities, so we now measure both separately.

\emph{Sampling noise} is what changes when only the $100$-observation draw changes. Three file-shuffle seeds on the frozen public ECoT-bridge checkpoint give $\alpha(\text{cot}) = 0.3434, 0.3443, 0.3444$: $\sigma = 0.057$\,pp, full range $0.10$\,pp, and no bucket exceeds $\sigma = 0.094$\,pp at this layer set (across all five layer sets in the depth sweep below the worst case is $\sigma = 0.26$\,pp, at layers $16$--$19$). Sampling noise at $N{=}100$ is therefore negligible --- roughly $25\times$ smaller than the spread we are trying to resolve --- and it is \emph{not} the reason within-ECoT differences are unresolvable.

\emph{Training-run noise} is what changes when the same configuration is trained again, which is the quantity leaderboard rows actually differ in. \textbf{Every trained row now has one}: we retrained all seven configurations from scratch at a byte-identical recipe and the same seed, and scored each replicate with the same 13-family protocol at the same evaluation seed on the same $100$ samples, so within a pair the only thing that differs is the training run. $|\Delta\alpha(\text{cot})|$ ranges over $0.12$, $0.14$, $0.56$, $0.56$, $0.73$, $1.45$, and $\mathbf{1.95}$\,pp (r=16, r=64, no-CoT, data-50B, data-50A, r=32, r=8). The $2.30$\,pp within-ECoT spread is therefore only $\mathbf{1.2\times}$ the largest same-config retraining difference --- \emph{less} margin than the $1.6\times$ the two-pair estimate reported, because the widest retraining gap in the benchmark belongs to a configuration that previously had no replicate at all. The conclusion is unchanged and now rests on a distribution rather than an anecdote: \textbf{no ordering among the seven ECoT variants is supported, including the no-CoT-vs-r=32 contrast, and all within-ECoT attention differences in this paper should be read as ties.} We still do not convert this into a significance test: seven pairs bound the noise, but one replicate per configuration estimates each pair's own difference with a single degree of freedom. The $23$--$29$\,pp cross-architecture gap is $12\times$ the largest training-run figure and is safe. The same protocol applied to $\mathcal{F}$ (all $9$ families at $N \geq 50$, per pair) gives mean $|\Delta\mathcal{F}|$ of $0.024$--$0.079$ and max $|\Delta\mathcal{F}|$ up to $\mathbf{0.260}$ (r=8, \emph{verb\_swap}), which is the error bar readers should attach to every single-run leaderboard cell --- and it is larger than most differences between rows.

\paragraph{The bucket ordering is an artifact of the layer choice.} Eq.~\ref{eq:attn} averages over $L = \{0,1,2,3\}$. That choice was justified in the submission only by an appeal to early cross-modal mixing, so we re-ran the identical measurement at four further layer sets --- $\{8..11\}$, $\{16..19\}$, $\{28..31\}$, and all $32$ --- at the same three seeds, for $5 \times 3 = 15$ runs of $N{=}100$ in total. The four buckets do not merely shift, \textbf{they reorder}, and the sweep localizes the effect much more sharply than the two endpoints alone could:

\begin{center}\small
\fitwidth{\columnwidth}{\begin{tabular}{lccccl}
\toprule
layers & $\alpha(\text{cot})$ & $\alpha(\text{visual})$ & $\alpha(\text{instr})$ & $\alpha(\text{prev})$ & ordering \\
\midrule
$0$--$3$ (reported)   & \textbf{0.344} & 0.290 & 0.300 & 0.065 & cot $>$ instr $>$ visual \\
$8$--$11$             & 0.157 & \textbf{0.428} & 0.336 & 0.079 & visual $>$ instr $>$ cot \\
$16$--$19$            & 0.212 & \textbf{0.412} & 0.309 & 0.067 & visual $>$ instr $>$ cot \\
$28$--$31$            & 0.262 & \textbf{0.455} & 0.227 & 0.056 & visual $>$ cot $>$ instr \\
all $32$              & 0.213 & \textbf{0.414} & 0.311 & 0.062 & visual $>$ instr $>$ cot \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

\noindent$\alpha(\text{cot})$ leads in \textbf{exactly one of the four four-layer blocks we probed --- and it is the block the submission reported}. It swings $18.7$\,pp across depth (min $0.157$ at layers $8$--$11$, max $0.344$ at layers $0$--$3$) against a worst-case three-seed sampling $\sigma$ of $0.26$\,pp: a ratio of $72\times$, so this is a depth effect and not a sample-draw effect. The variation is also \emph{not monotone} --- $\alpha(\text{cot})$ falls to its minimum in the early-middle of the network and then recovers toward the output layers --- so ``deeper layers attend less to the CoT'' would also be the wrong summary. \textbf{The statement ``the CoT segment receives the largest share of action-token attention'' is true in the first four layers and false in every other block we measured.} Combined with the per-token normalization of Section~\ref{sec:analysis} --- where the CoT bucket is largest only because it is longest --- the apparent prominence of the CoT segment fails two independent robustness checks. We keep the layer-$0$--$3$ numbers as the primary ones for continuity with the submitted tables and because early-layer mixing is where a routing effect would be expected, but F1 and F3 should be read as claims about early-layer attention specifically, and we advise against reporting any bucket ordering without stating the layer set. Since the ordering our reported layer set produces is the one that does \emph{not} generalize, we treat the layer set as part of the claim rather than as a presentation choice, and release all $15$ runs. This is a defect in how P1 was specified, not in the measurement; it does not touch P2, which is causal rather than attributional.

\subsubsection{F2: Causal effect requires reasoning-target training}

Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} contrasts the no-CoT variant against the six CoT-trained variants of the same base and data. The no-CoT model's Faithfulness Score collapses across every semantic tier -- direction\_flip $\mathcal{F}\!=\!0.274$ vs CoT-trained $\mathcal{F}\!\in\![0.66, 0.82]$; verb\_swap $\mathcal{F}\!=\!0.163$ vs $\mathcal{F}\!\in\![0.52, 0.84]$; cross\_task\_swap (upper-bound control) $\mathcal{F}\!=\!0.260$ vs $\mathcal{F}\!\in\![0.73, 0.94]$ (the no-CoT figures are 3-seed means, matching Table~\ref{tab:calibration}; an earlier version quoted the seed-0 values $0.23/0.14/0.24$ here and the 3-seed means in the table). \textbf{F2: Reasoning-target training is what makes CoT causally load-bearing on manipulation actions} --- \emph{in absolute terms}. The next subsection shows that this is the weaker of two available readings, and that the stronger one does not survive calibration.

\subsubsection{F2 calibrated: the no-CoT collapse is a uniform gain reduction, not selective CoT-insensitivity}
\label{sec:f2_calib}

The F2 statement above compares raw $\mathcal{F}$ across models. That comparison is confounded by a per-model nuisance quantity: how much a given checkpoint's decoded action moves under \emph{any} prompt perturbation at all. The no-CoT variant does not merely score low on semantic families --- it also scores low on \emph{cross\_task\_swap}, the family we designated the maximum-effect control by replacing the entire trace with an unrelated task's reasoning. If the metric's own ceiling has moved down for that model, part of the observed ``collapse'' is a change in scale rather than a change in CoT sensitivity.

We therefore normalize each model's mean magnitude score by its own control ceiling, $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{norm}}(m) = \bar{\mathcal{F}}(m) / \mathcal{F}(m, \text{cross\_task\_swap})$, which asks what fraction of the effect this model is \emph{capable} of showing is actually elicited by semantic edits. The result reverses the interpretation for the model F2 rests on. Every row below is now a 3-sampling-seed mean from that model's own 13-family run, so the floor row --- absent from the submitted version of this table --- is measured rather than assumed (all values from \texttt{results\_\allowbreak{}v2/\allowbreak{}derived\_\allowbreak{}metrics.json}):

\begin{center}\small
\fitwidth{\columnwidth}{\begin{tabular}{lccccccc}
\toprule
& no-CoT & r=8 & r=16 & r=32 & r=64 & data-50A & data-50B \\
\midrule
$\bar{\mathcal{F}}$ (raw) & 0.166 & 0.407 & 0.446 & 0.395 & 0.514 & 0.393 & 0.353 \\
$\mathcal{F}(\text{cross\_task\_swap})$ (ceiling) & 0.260 & 0.857 & 0.883 & 0.810 & 0.887 & 0.730 & 0.733 \\
$\mathcal{F}(\text{paraphrase\_null})$ (floor) & 0.193 & 0.587 & 0.547 & 0.567 & 0.657 & 0.537 & 0.447 \\
\midrule
$\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{norm}}$ (one-sided) & \textbf{0.637} & 0.475 & 0.505 & 0.487 & 0.580 & 0.538 & 0.481 \\
two-sided & $-0.416$ & $-0.665$ & $-0.299$ & $-0.706$ & $-0.621$ & $-0.743$ & $-0.327$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

\textbf{The action-only model has the \emph{highest} ceiling-normalized score of the seven same-base variants (0.637 vs 0.475--0.580).} Relative to the response it is able to produce, the no-CoT model is not less sensitive to CoT semantics than the CoT-trained models; it is \emph{uniformly less responsive to the CoT segment as a whole}, semantic and maximal edits alike, by a factor of roughly $3.1\times$ (its ceiling is $0.260$ against a mean of $0.817$ for the other six). So the defensible version of F2 is a statement about absolute effect size, useful to a practitioner asking ``will editing the CoT move this policy at all,'' and it is \emph{not} evidence that reasoning-target training induces specifically semantic CoT$\to$action routing. We restate it that way and drop the stronger claim. (ECoT-bridge reaches $\bar{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{norm}} = 0.892$ on the same leaderboard run, but Section~\ref{sec:paraphrase_null} shows that number is itself uninterpretable as semantic sensitivity, because its paraphrase floor sits at the same height as its ceiling.)

\paragraph{The two-sided row is the one to read, and it is negative on all seven.} Ceiling normalization removes the scale confound but not the surface-form confound: it divides by the ceiling and ignores the floor. The submitted version of this table could not be recomputed two-sided, because no ``ours'' variant had a measured floor. All seven now do, and the correction does not shrink the one-sided numbers --- \textbf{it flips their sign}. Every one-sided value sits in $[0.475, 0.637]$, which reads as ``semantic edits elicit roughly half the effect this model can show''; every two-sided value is \emph{negative}, from $-0.299$ to $-0.743$, which says the same edits elicit \emph{less} than a meaning-preserving paraphrase of the same trace does. That is not a $4.4\times$ overstatement of a positive quantity, as we described it when one row was calibrated; it is a positive-looking score for a quantity that is actually below its own null on every row we can now check. We keep the one-sided row because it is what the submitted F2 rests on and withdrawing it silently would hide the correction, but \textbf{the one-sided ordering must not be read as floor-corrected, and no ordering should be read off either row} --- see limitation (iii). The one two-sided positive anywhere in this paper is the independent retraining of the no-CoT variant ($+0.127$; Table~\ref{tab:calibration}), i.e.\ the model that was trained not to use its CoT, which is the behaviour a working floor-corrected statistic should produce there.

\paragraph{What the sweep was designed to answer, and what it answered.} We flagged the concrete way F2 could dissolve outright: if the out-of-CoT control \emph{instr\_random\_sub} outscores the CoT families on the ``ours'' variants as it does on ECoT-bridge ($0.99$, above every CoT family), then the no-CoT-vs-CoT-trained contrast underlying F2 is a contrast in \emph{global prompt sensitivity} rather than in CoT routing. The stated survival condition was $\bar{\mathcal{F}} > \mathcal{F}(\text{instr\_random\_sub})$ for the CoT-trained variants and \emph{not} for no-CoT. The sweep has now run, and \textbf{the sign of that contrast is as F2 predicts}: the ratio $\bar{\mathcal{F}}/\mathcal{F}(\text{instr\_random\_sub})$ is above one on $5$ of the $6$ CoT-trained variants (r=8 $1.222$, r=16 $1.022$, r=32 $1.067$, r=64 $1.028$, data-50B $1.307$; data-50A is $0.907$) and below one on no-CoT ($0.629$), exactly the direction required. \textbf{F2 therefore does not dissolve.} But it does not clear the bar we set for reading effect sizes either: retraining a configuration from scratch moves $\bar{\mathcal{F}}$ by up to $0.092$ (Section~\ref{sec:analysis}, seven same-config pairs), and \textbf{not one of the five clears the out-of-CoT control by more than that}. The two largest margins, data-50B ($+0.083$) and r=8 ($+0.074$), sit just under it; r=32 ($+0.025$), r=64 ($+0.014$) and r=16 ($+0.009$) are far inside it. The ordering of that list is itself a warning: the configuration with the widest apparent margin, data-50B, is also the one whose own retraining moves $\bar{\mathcal{F}}$ the most ($0.092$), which is what a margin drawn from run-to-run variation rather than from CoT routing looks like. So the result is \textbf{robust in direction on the family and inside the retraining error bar on every one of its six members}, and the correct reading of F2 is the absolute-effect-size statement above, now with a measured floor under it rather than a promissory note. An earlier revision of this paragraph put two of the six outside that bar; it was measuring against a floor estimated from two retraining pairs instead of seven.

\subsubsection{F3: Attention distribution does not predict causal effect}

Figure~\ref{fig:dissociation}\,(a) shows CoT attention $\alpha(m, \text{cot})$ for the eight trained variants (7 ``ours'' + 1 ECoT-bridge); all sit within $\alpha(m, \text{cot}) \in [0.335, 0.358]$ (max--min gap $=0.023$). Panel (b) shows the mean Faithfulness Score over seven non-control edit families; the same models span $\bar{\mathcal{F}}\in[0.166, 0.860]$, a $5.2\times$ gap (Wilson 95\% CIs on the two extremes, over the $N{=}612$ records the seven non-control families contribute: no-CoT $\bar{\mathcal{F}}{=}0.166 \in [0.140, 0.199]$; ECoT-bridge $\bar{\mathcal{F}}{=}0.860 \in [0.834, 0.888]$ --- CIs disjoint by $>0.63$). The metric's null (selfsplice) is $\mathcal{F}\!=\!0.000$ across all eight trained models (Wilson 95\% CI $[0.00, 0.06]$ at $N{=}60$), ruling out tokenization noise as an alternative explanation. \textbf{F3: Attention distribution does not predict causal effect.}

\paragraph{The withdrawn P3 run, and the audit that withdrew it.} We had additionally probed whether attention on the CoT segment predicts \emph{per-sample action error} via a Mann--Whitney AUROC, and previously reported $\alpha(m,\text{cot}){=}0.410$, $\alpha(m,\text{visual}){=}0.607$, $\alpha(m,\text{instruction}){=}0.459$, $\alpha(m,\text{action-prev}){=}0.644$ on $N{=}200$. \textbf{Those AUROCs are not interpretable and we withdraw them}; the corrected in-domain re-run is Section~\ref{sec:p3_indomain}, and it does not reproduce them. The run evaluated \texttt{ecot-openvla-7b-bridge} --- a Bridge-trained model --- against \emph{LIBERO} ground-truth actions while de-normalizing with \texttt{bridge\_orig} statistics. This is a cross-domain comparison on two independent axes (percentile normalization and gripper polarity convention), and the resulting ``error'' signal is dominated by a fixed domain offset rather than by model error. The diagnostics we now publish alongside the logs (\texttt{scripts/\allowbreak{}decoder\_\allowbreak{}audit.py}) make this unambiguous: predicted and ground-truth actions are \emph{anti}-correlated (pooled $r{=}-0.692$; $r_{\text{dim}0}{=}-0.419$, $r_{\text{dim}1}{=}-0.600$), the gripper dimension has predicted mean $+0.976$ against a ground-truth constant $-1.0$ (sign agreement $2\%$), and the model's action L$_1$ of $0.597$ is worse than both trivial baselines by a wide margin (predict-zero $0.190$; predict-the-dataset-mean-action $0.046$, i.e.\ $13\times$ better than the model). An AUROC computed over such a ranking measures the domain offset, not reasoning fidelity.

We therefore adopt a \textbf{published decoder-validation gate}: no probe that compares decoded actions against ground-truth demonstrations enters CoT-Faith unless (i) the model is evaluated in the corpus it was trained on, (ii) per-dimension $\mathrm{corr}(\hat a, a)$ is reported, and (iii) the model's L$_1$ beats predict-per-dim-mean. \textbf{No F1--F6 claim in this paper depends on P3}, because $\Delta_\infty$ is a \emph{self}-comparison between $a(s,\text{cot})$ and $a(s,f(\text{cot}))$ decoded by the same model under the same statistics, so any fixed normalization offset cancels exactly.

\subsubsection{P3, re-run in-domain: correcting the protocol does not recover a predictor}
\label{sec:p3_indomain}
The re-run holds the model, the four attention channels and the median-split labelling fixed and changes only what the withdrawal was about. It scores \texttt{ecot-openvla-7b-bridge} on \textbf{Bridge~V2}, the corpus it was trained on, and it un-normalizes the predicted action with that checkpoint's own $q_{01}/q_{99}$ for \texttt{bridge\_orig} before differencing it against the demonstration, with the gripper dimension passed through unrescaled as its \texttt{mask=False} entry requires. Bridge ships no ground-truth reasoning, so the CoT is self-generated on all samples --- which is also the only condition a deployed failure predictor is ever in. The loader yielded $N{=}153$ usable frames of the $200$ requested.

\textbf{The protocol error was not a source of noise; it was the dominant term.} Median action L$_1$ is $0.0199$ in robot units under the corrected protocol against $0.2550$ under the withdrawn one --- a factor of $12.8$ --- and \textbf{$40$ of the $153$ samples change their high-versus-low-error label} between the two. The withdrawn AUROCs were therefore not a noisy estimate of the corrected ones; they were computed over a different labelling.

Table~\ref{tab:p3} gives the result. We report the \emph{raw} AUROC with a $10{,}000$-draw bootstrap over samples, re-deriving the median split within each draw. \textbf{The channel a CoT-faithfulness claim would need --- $\alpha(m,\text{cot})$ --- does not separate high-error from low-error frames} ($0.596$, 95\% CI $[0.491, 0.679]$). One channel does: $\alpha(m,\text{instruction})$ at $0.362$, CI $[0.284, 0.469]$, which survives Bonferroni correction across the four channels ($98.75\%$ CI $[0.261, 0.493]$). Its direction is that \emph{low} attention on the instruction predicts \emph{high} action error, which is at least a sensible failure mode --- a policy that stops reading the command errs --- but we read that direction off these same $153$ samples, so it is a description of this run and not a pre-registered prediction. Notably, the withdrawn protocol moved exactly that channel to $0.492$: the defect destroyed the one signal present.

Two reporting points belong with the table. First, our earlier summary of this probe as ``AUROC $=0.50$, all four features at chance'' was right in conclusion and wrong in derivation, and we no longer state it that way. Second, the report also carries $|\text{AUROC}-0.5|$, which is convenient for ranking channels by effect size but is \emph{biased away from $0.5$ by construction}: bootstrapping $\max(r, 1-r)$ puts the lower bound above $0.5$ even for a pure-noise channel, and all four channels' folded intervals ``exclude chance'' for that reason alone. Only the raw column tests anything, and we make the audit script assert on the raw column.

So P3 returns to the paper as a specified probe with a measured negative result rather than as a withdrawal.

\paragraph{The gate also fails on our own checkpoint, and that constrains how Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} may be read.} Criterion (iii) was written to disqualify other people's probes and it disqualifies ours too. Running the same decoder audit in-domain on the \mbox{r=32} LIBERO fine-tune behind six of the eight leaderboard rows (\texttt{auroc\_\allowbreak{}indomain\_\allowbreak{}ours\_\allowbreak{}null/\allowbreak{}}, $N{=}200$, released with this paper) returns \texttt{frame\_\allowbreak{}check.passed = false}: its open-loop single-step L$_1$ is $0.0486$ against $0.0457$ for predicting the per-dimension dataset mean, a ratio of $1.063$, and \emph{no} frame the checkpoint ships does better --- the report's own diagnosis is that this is a competence result and not a units error. \textbf{Six of eight leaderboard rows therefore come from a policy whose single-step open-loop prediction does not beat a constant.} We disclose this rather than leave it in the release unmentioned, and we state what it does and does not undermine. It does not invalidate $\Delta_\infty$: every $\mathcal{F}$ in this paper is a \emph{self}-comparison between $a(s,\text{cot})$ and $a(s,f(\text{cot}))$ decoded by the same model under the same statistics, so it never references a ground-truth demonstration and a policy can be poor in absolute terms while still changing its output measurably under an edit. What it does undermine is any reading of Table~\ref{tab:leaderboard} as a statement about competent policies, and it is the direct cause of the missing rollout evidence in limitation~(v). A reader should treat those rows as edit-sensitivity measurements on weak policies, which is one more reason the table is a diagnostic rather than a ranking.

That is a weaker claim than the one the original run appeared to license and a stronger one than silence: on the single model where we can run it in-domain, per-sample CoT attention carries no usable signal about per-sample action error, which is consistent with F3's dissociation of attention from causal effect measured by an entirely different route.

\paragraph{The rollout gate: four failures, three causes, and a pass.} Our earlier diagnostic rollout of the public \texttt{openvla-7b-finetuned-libero-spatial} checkpoint returned Task SR $=0/20$ against a published ${\sim}85\%$. That number was a \emph{scoring} defect in our harness: success was read from \texttt{info["success"]}, a key LIBERO never populates, so the episode loop terminated on task completion and then recorded the episode as a failure --- Task SR was structurally pinned at $0$ regardless of behaviour. A second attempt was invalidated by an initial-state loader that read \texttt{.pruned\_init} \texttt{torch.save} archives with \texttt{np.load} and silently fell back to a random \texttt{env.reset()}. Both bugs are fixed; the loader now raises rather than falling back, a unit test asserts that on garbage input, and every rollout report records how many episodes used canonical initial states.

Table~\ref{tab:gate} is the pre-fix baseline everything below is measured against: what the harness scored once those two bugs were fixed and before any of the upstream differences were found. $200$ episodes, $50$ per suite, $50/50$ on canonical initial states in every case, and \textbf{it did not reproduce the published SR}. Three suites are interpretable; \emph{libero\_10} is excluded because we ran a flat $400$-step budget everywhere and upstream allots that suite $520$, so its $0/50$ can be truncation rather than failure and we do not quote it as evidence. The best interpretable cell is \emph{libero\_goal} at $5/50 = 0.10$ against a published $0.794$. The gate as it now stands --- after three causes were found, the third of them only by abandoning the diff-and-reason loop --- is Table~\ref{tab:gate_pass}, and it passes; the two paragraphs in between are the search, reported in the order it happened because three of its four steps were nulls and the nulls are what narrowed it.

That the failure is \emph{degraded rather than impossible} is what let us localize it. A control channel that is simply wrong would pin every suite at exactly zero; $0.10$ on one suite instead indicates a policy operating on slightly off-distribution inputs. Rather than continue guessing --- four gate attempts had each spent GPU-hours to learn only ``still ${\approx}0$'' --- we diffed our harness against \texttt{openvla/openvla} at the source level (\texttt{experiments/\allowbreak{}openvla\_\allowbreak{}reference\_\allowbreak{}diff.py}, run on a networked host so the comparison is against upstream's actual code and not our recollection of it). It found exactly two differences live in the Table~\ref{tab:gate} runs. First, the gripper channel: upstream composes \texttt{normalize\_\allowbreak{}gripper\_\allowbreak{}action(binarize=True)} with \texttt{invert\_gripper\_action}, i.e.\ $g \mapsto -\operatorname{sign}(2g-1)$, and we passed $g$ through unchanged. Second, and on no hypothesis list we had written beforehand, image preprocessing: upstream's \texttt{resize\_image} applies a JPEG encode/decode round-trip ``as done in RLDS dataset builder'' and then \texttt{tf.image.resize(method="lanczos3",\allowbreak{} antialias=True)} to $224$, explicitly ``to make input images in distribution with respect to the inputs seen at training time''; we handed the raw $256{\times}256$ render to the processor. A per-frame compression-and-kernel mismatch degrades a policy without making success impossible, which is the signature we measured.

\emph{The gripper convention alone is not the cause, and we report that as a result rather than dropping it.} Before spending GPU-hours on the two-factor grid we ran the gripper factor by itself, on the suite that discriminates it most sharply: every \emph{libero\_object} task is a pick-and-place, so success there is impossible without a working gripper. Four conventions --- identity, $-g$, binarize-then-invert, and upstream's $g \mapsto -\operatorname{sign}(2g{-}1)$ --- ran under one model load, $10$ episodes each, $40$ episodes in total and all $40$ on canonical initial states. The arms are verifiably distinct rather than four runs of one configuration: the mean gripper command actually delivered to the simulator spans $-0.535$ to $+0.7795$ across them, and the fraction of closed-gripper commands moves from $0.12$ to $0.89$. All four scored $0/10$. The scope of that null matters and the tempting reading of it is wrong in a specific way: the source diff establishes that upstream's convention differs from ours, so a uniform zero rules out that this difference is \emph{sufficient} to explain the gate --- not that it is a non-difference. Any correction that closes the gap must therefore contain the gripper fix \emph{and} something else, which is what promoted image preprocessing from a hypothesis on nobody's list to the leading one. The artifact is released verbatim at \texttt{results\_\allowbreak{}v2/\allowbreak{}canonical\_\allowbreak{}runs/\allowbreak{}gripper\_\allowbreak{}ab\_\allowbreak{}null/\allowbreak{}}, including its own caveats: the run's own report printed the \emph{requested} $4$ episodes per arm beside a realised $10$ (episodes-per-task floors at $1$ so that no task is skipped, and \emph{libero\_object} has $10$ tasks), and the job's non-zero exit is the script's designed signal for ``no arm clears the threshold'' rather than a crash --- a null that exited $0$ would be indistinguishable from a fix.

Both differences are now implemented behind named configuration arms and measured factorially against the Table~\ref{tab:gate} configuration as the anchor cell. \textbf{The factorial is also a null: all four cells scored $0/10$}, including the cell that applies both corrections at once (\texttt{gripper=openvla}, \texttt{image=pil\_lanczos}). It ran on \emph{libero\_object} at upstream's own $280$-step budget for that suite --- so truncation, which was on our candidate list, is excluded by construction --- with $10$ episodes per cell, $40$ in total, all $40$ on canonical initial states, under one model load and with no cell raising. The cells are again verifiably distinct: the gripper factor moves the mean delivered gripper command from $+0.216$ to $+0.753$ and the closed-gripper fraction from $0.695$ to $0.876$, and the image factor perturbs both slightly in the direction a changed input distribution would. So the position we are in is precise and worth stating rather than smoothing over: reading upstream's source found two genuine differences, and measurement has now shown that neither of them, nor their conjunction, is what the gate is failing on. We then repeated the whole factorial with upstream's \emph{exact} preprocessing --- \texttt{tensorflow}'s own \texttt{encode\_jpeg}, \texttt{decode\_image} and \texttt{resize} rather than our $8/255$-LSB reimplementation --- because the hypothesis under test was that a small per-frame input mismatch degrades the policy, and testing it with a path that itself carries a small per-frame mismatch leaves ``the approximation was not close enough'' available as an excuse for the null. It is not available: the exact run reproduces the same $0/10$ in all four cells, with its \texttt{gripper=openvla} anchor agreeing with the approximate run's to every printed digit. That run also settles the tensorflow question in production rather than in a probe --- a full 7B-model GPU rollout with \texttt{tensorflow} imported in the same process, using CUDA throughout. \emph{The last candidate is now closed too, and it is the first non-null in this investigation.} What remained was the action de-quantization --- the one quantity in this harness validated only by our own offline audit rather than against upstream's code path. Rather than diff our reimplementation against upstream's source and reason about it, which is what had produced four failures already, we called the \texttt{predict\_action} the checkpoint ships in its own remote code --- the method the published SR was measured with --- on real trajectory frames with our decoder driving the arm, and compared numbers. \textbf{The two decoders agree on $0$ of $24$ frames}: max L$_\infty$ $1.122$, mean per-frame L$_\infty$ $0.719$, and Pearson $r$ near zero in every dimension ($+0.23$, $+0.60$, $+0.03$, $-0.15$, $-0.31$, $+0.20$ from $x$ through yaw). The per-timestep L$_\infty$ is flat over $t{=}0\ldots7$, so this is a wrong function and not a drift. The gripper channel makes the mechanism readable: on those frames the arm has not reached the object and the correct command is a constant hold-open, and upstream emits exactly one value on all $24$ (the top bin, $0.9961$, std $0$) while ours emits $11$ distinct values from $-0.126$ to $+0.996$ (std $0.380$). This is not an artifact of the image failing to reach upstream's method --- it produces $18$ distinct actions over the $24$ frames, so it is frame-sensitive, and only the gripper is pinned, which is the dimension that should be pinned here --- and it independently reproduces, now with the mechanism exposed, what \texttt{decoder\_audit.json} recorded offline as $2\%$ gripper sign agreement against ${\sim}50\%$ chance. Two consequences, one of which costs us the framing above. First, \textbf{the three earlier nulls must be restated}: each tested its factor \emph{on top of our decode}, so each bounds insufficiency conditional on a decode now measured to be wrong. In particular upstream's $g \mapsto -\operatorname{sign}(2g{-}1)$ was applied to a channel it was never written for, which is why the follow-up run crosses the decoder axis with the gripper axis rather than adding a sixth factor to the list. Second, the arithmetic is exonerated and the token selection is not: both decoders' values land on legal centres of \texttt{linspace}$(-1,1,256)$ to $4.7{\times}10^{-7}$ and they share exact values in $x$, $y$ and $z$, so the bin grid \emph{and} the un-normalization agree, and the residual difference is in which tokens get selected --- our hand-rolled seven-step masked-argmax loop against upstream's own \texttt{generate} with its input-id surgery. \texttt{norm\_stats} key resolution is likewise not the whole story, since the gripper dimension carries \texttt{mask=False} in every OpenVLA \texttt{norm\_stats} and so bypasses un-normalization entirely. Artifact: \texttt{results\_\allowbreak{}v2/\allowbreak{}canonical\_\allowbreak{}runs/\allowbreak{}action\_\allowbreak{}decode\_\allowbreak{}mismatch/\allowbreak{}}. \emph{The last unexcluded cause was the token selection, and replacing it is what closed the gate.} The bin grid and the un-normalization are exonerated above and the two decoders share exact values in $x$, $y$ and $z$, so what remained was which tokens our hand-rolled masked-argmax loop selects against upstream's \texttt{generate} with its input-id surgery. The same question for the \emph{published} path had already been answered separately and in the metric's favour --- P2's own selection is byte-identical to upstream's on $66/66$ prompts (\texttt{p2\_decode\_equivalence}, next paragraph) --- so the defect was localized to the rollout harness. We then stopped diffing that loop against upstream and deleted it: the rollout now calls the \texttt{predict\_action} the checkpoint ships in its own remote code, behind \texttt{action\_\allowbreak{}decoder=upstream}, and the gate was re-run on top of it. \textbf{The third cause was the action decode itself}, and the result is Table~\ref{tab:gate_pass}, reported next. Artifacts: \texttt{results\_\allowbreak{}v2/\allowbreak{}canonical\_\allowbreak{}runs/\allowbreak{}gate\_\allowbreak{}factorial\_\allowbreak{}pil/\allowbreak{}} and \texttt{gate\_factorial\_tf/}. One methodological point is worth reporting because it changed our implementation three times, the last time by retiring a constraint we had never checked. Our repository asserted that the eval environment cannot host \texttt{tensorflow} --- that installing it displaces the \texttt{numpy}${<}2$ pin the OpenVLA stack requires and breaks \texttt{transformers}' lazy TF detection --- so we reimplemented upstream's preprocessing and measured the reimplementation against \texttt{tensorflow} in an isolated environment rather than trusting it. The first substitute, Pillow's \texttt{LANCZOS}, disagreed by up to $23/255$ intensity levels against a $4$-level ceiling fixed in advance, so we discarded it and implemented the Lanczos-3 kernel directly. Crucially we measured the JPEG step and the resize step \emph{separately}, since an aggregate figure does not say which one is wrong: the kernel agrees with \texttt{tf.image.resize} to within $1/255$, i.e.\ exactly up to \texttt{uint8} rounding, while the JPEG round-trip carries the entire residual, and a sweep of Pillow's chroma-subsampling setting against \texttt{tf.image.encode\_jpeg} showed $4{:}4{:}4$ off by $240$ levels, $4{:}2{:}2$ by $150$, and $4{:}2{:}0$ by $9$ --- our first version had defaulted to $4{:}4{:}4$ on the plausible-but-irrelevant reasoning that less downsampling is closer to the original render. With that corrected the full path sits $8/255$ from upstream (mean $0.6$--$1.4$), the residual being a Pillow-versus-\texttt{tensorflow} \texttt{libjpeg} disagreement that no Pillow setting closes. We then went back and tested the constraint that had forced the reimplementation in the first place, because an $8/255$ approximation is defensible but a measured zero is better and the cost of finding out was one CPU job: both halves of it are false. Installing \texttt{tensorflow-cpu} left \texttt{numpy} at $1.26.4$, left \texttt{torch} with CUDA and a correct \texttt{matmul}, and \texttt{transformers} reports \texttt{is\_tf\_available()} as false under \texttt{USE\_TF=0}. The exact factorial reported above therefore calls upstream's own \texttt{tensorflow} ops and is exact by construction rather than approximate, and it ran to completion on a GPU host with \texttt{tensorflow} imported alongside \texttt{torch} in one process, which is the probe's conclusion holding in production rather than in isolation; the reimplementation remains as the fallback for environments without the dependency, with its $8/255$ cost measured rather than assumed. We report this because the misleading artifact was not a wrong measurement but an unmeasured assertion sitting in a comment, which had shaped the design for as long as it went unchallenged. The validation job imports the shipped function by path rather than a transcription of it, and asserts that the shipped subsampling default equals the measured-best value, which is how the $4{:}4{:}4$ error was caught at all. \textbf{No number elsewhere in this paper is conditioned on a rollout}, and Section~\ref{sec:limitations}\,(v) states precisely what a passing gate would and would not license.

\paragraph{The gate passes, and both corrections are necessary for it to.} Table~\ref{tab:gate_pass} is the gate re-run at that composition: the checkpoint's own \texttt{predict\_action} in place of our masked-argmax loop, with upstream's $g \mapsto -\operatorname{sign}(2g{-}1)$ gripper convention applied on top of it. \textbf{Task SR moves from $0.00/0.00/0.10$ to $0.74/0.90/0.74$ on \emph{libero\_spatial}/\emph{libero\_object}/\emph{libero\_goal}, and \emph{libero\_10} --- excluded from Table~\ref{tab:gate} as uninterpretable --- comes in at $0.46$} --- $0.877$, $1.022$, $0.932$ and $0.853$ of each suite's published SR, against a criterion of one half fixed before the run. \textbf{The gate therefore passes on all four suites upstream publishes a LIBERO checkpoint for, which is the whole gate rather than a subset of it} (see limitation (ix): there is no \emph{libero\_90} checkpoint and hence no published SR to gate against). Three of the four Wilson intervals contain the published value outright; \emph{libero\_spatial}'s upper limit is $0.841$ against a published $0.844$, so it falls just short of containing it and we quote it that way rather than as agreement. Three conditions make this a gate rather than a demonstration and each is recorded per suite in the artifact. Every suite ran at \emph{upstream's own} step budget ($220$, $280$, $300$, $520$), requested through the \texttt{MAX\_STEPS=0} sentinel rather than the flat $400$ the pre-fix table used, so no cell was bought with extra time and \textbf{the truncation caveat that excluded \emph{libero\_10} from Table~\ref{tab:gate} is retired by measurement}: that suite now runs at the $520$ steps upstream allots it and scores $23/50$ rather than $0/50$. All $50/50$ episodes in every arm ran on the suite's canonical initial state. And each job carries its own \emph{anchor} arm under the same model load, holding the corrected decoder and dropping only the gripper convention: it scores $0.00$, $0.00$, $0.12$ and $0.00$. So the decoder fix alone is not sufficient on any suite, the earlier factorial had already shown the gripper fix alone is not sufficient ($0/10$ in every cell, on top of the decode now known to be wrong), and \textbf{joint necessity is measured here rather than argued}, now on four suites including the longest-horizon one. The arms are verifiably distinct in the channel that separates them --- within the winning arm the mean gripper command actually delivered to the simulator is transformed from $+0.447$ to $+0.102$ on \emph{spatial}, $+0.441$ to $+0.115$ on \emph{object}, $+0.717$ to $-0.440$ on \emph{goal} and $+0.587$ to $-0.179$ on \emph{libero\_10}, while in the anchor arm the delivered command is the raw one by construction. One incidental corroboration is worth recording because it is the signal the original \texttt{info["success"]} bug destroyed: the winning arms collect $7{,}025$/$7{,}864$/$7{,}931$/$20{,}577$ gripper samples against the anchors' $11{,}000$/$14{,}000$/$13{,}897$/$26{,}000$, i.e.\ the episodes are \emph{shorter} exactly where they are scored successful, so the success flag and the episode length now agree, and on all four suites. Two things this does and does not license. It establishes that the public checkpoint is competent at the task inside our harness, which retires the harness as a candidate explanation for anything else in this paper and retires the ``we do not claim the decoder is validated at the rollout level'' hedge that four previous versions of this section carried. It does \emph{not} make any published number rollout-conditioned --- every $\mathcal{F}$ here is still a first-step paired-intervention quantity, and whether those deltas are correctly scaled is a separate question settled separately in the next paragraph. We also note what the pass does \emph{not} contain: \texttt{image\_preproc} is \texttt{none} in the winning composition, so upstream's JPEG-plus-lanczos3 frame preprocessing --- a genuine difference from upstream, implemented and measured to $8/255$ and then to exactness --- turns out not to be needed for the gate at this $N$. It stays in the harness as a configurable arm; it is not part of the fix. Artifact: \texttt{results\_\allowbreak{}v2/\allowbreak{}canonical\_\allowbreak{}runs/\allowbreak{}gate\_\allowbreak{}foursuite\_\allowbreak{}winning/\allowbreak{}}, one directory per suite with its compute-platform task id.
